A trained model is just a file. To be useful it needs a **door**: something that accepts a request, prepares the input, calls the model and sends back an answer. This article shows the tools that build that door, using **PayGuard**, our fraud model from the [overview](/deployment/deployment-overview.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn
- The four layers of a serving stack and the tool for each layer
- How to wrap a model in a FastAPI service in about 30 lines
- How to track and register models with MLflow
- Why sending rows in batches can be many times faster, measured live
:::

{{< include ../_series-nav.md >}}

## Four layers, four jobs

Think of serving as a stack. Each layer answers one question. Pick a layer to see its tools.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {ms, msStyle} from "/assets/js/ms-plot.js"
layers = [
  {name: "Track and register", q: "Which model version is this, and how was it trained?", tools: "MLflow, Weights & Biases, Neptune", c: ms.violet},
  {name: "Package", q: "How do I save the model so it loads anywhere?", tools: "joblib, ONNX, TorchScript, SavedModel, Docker", c: ms.indigo},
  {name: "Serve", q: "How do requests reach the model?", tools: "FastAPI, BentoML, Ray Serve, NVIDIA Triton, KServe", c: ms.teal},
  {name: "Demo and test", q: "How do people try it before production?", tools: "Gradio, Streamlit, pytest, Locust", c: ms.amber}
]
viewof sel = Inputs.radio(layers.map(d => d.name), {value: "Serve", label: "Layer"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = 760, h = 58;
  const L = layers.find(d => d.name === sel);
  return htl.html`<div>${htl.svg`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${layers.length * (h + 10) + 10}" style="width:100%;max-width:${W}px;font-family:Inter,system-ui,sans-serif">
    ${layers.map((d, i) => htl.svg`<g>
      <rect x="${d.name === sel ? 10 : 40}" y="${10 + i * (h + 10)}" width="${d.name === sel ? W - 20 : W - 80}" height="${h}" rx="12" fill="${d.c}" fill-opacity="${d.name === sel ? 0.9 : 0.22}"/>
      <text x="${W / 2}" y="${10 + i * (h + 10) + h / 2 + 5}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" font-weight="600" fill="${d.name === sel ? "white" : "currentColor"}">${d.name}</text></g>`)}
  </svg>`}
  <div class="ms-readout"><span>${L.q}</span><b style="font-size:1.05rem">${L.tools}</b></div></div>`;
}
```

| Tool | Best at | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| **FastAPI** | Lightweight Python web APIs with automatic validation and docs | You want full control and a small, simple service |
| **BentoML** | Packaging a model plus its code into a deployable service | You want batching, containers and serving built in |
| **MLflow** | Experiment tracking, model registry, standard model format | You train many versions and need to know which is live |
| **ONNX Runtime** | Fast, framework-neutral inference | You need speed or want to run on edge devices |
| **NVIDIA Triton** | High-throughput GPU serving of many models | You serve deep learning models on GPUs at scale |
| **Ray Serve / KServe** | Scaling many models on a cluster | You already run Ray or Kubernetes |
| **Gradio / Streamlit** | Quick demo web pages | You want stakeholders to try the model |

## Step 1: train and save PayGuard

We simulate 20,000 card payments with a few features, train a gradient-boosted model and save it with `joblib`. This runs on any laptop.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, joblib, os
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 20_000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "amount": rng.lognormal(3.5, 1.0, n),          # dollars
    "hour": rng.integers(0, 24, n),
    "km_from_home": rng.exponential(15, n),
    "tx_last_hour": rng.poisson(1.2, n),
    "new_merchant": rng.binomial(1, 0.25, n),
})
# simulated fraud risk: big, late-night, far-away, rapid-fire payments
logit = (-6 + 0.012 * df.amount + 0.9 * (df.hour < 5)
         + 0.02 * df.km_from_home + 0.6 * df.tx_last_hour + 0.8 * df.new_merchant)
df["fraud"] = rng.binomial(1, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit)))

X, y = df.drop(columns="fraud"), df.fraud
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
model = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=200).fit(Xtr, ytr)
auc = roc_auc_score(yte, model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1])

os.makedirs("models", exist_ok=True)
joblib.dump(model, "models/payguard.joblib")
print(f"Fraud rate {y.mean():.1%}, test AUC {auc:.3f}")
```

## Step 2: give it a door with FastAPI

FastAPI checks every request against a schema, so a missing field returns a clear error instead of a crash. It also creates interactive documentation at `/docs`.

```{.python filename="app.py"}
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
import joblib, pandas as pd

model = joblib.load("models/payguard.joblib")   # load once, at start-up
app = FastAPI(title="PayGuard", version="1.0.0")

class Payment(BaseModel):
    amount: float = Field(gt=0)
    hour: int = Field(ge=0, le=23)
    km_from_home: float = Field(ge=0)
    tx_last_hour: int = Field(ge=0)
    new_merchant: int = Field(ge=0, le=1)

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}

@app.post("/score")
def score(payments: list[Payment]):
    X = pd.DataFrame([p.model_dump() for p in payments])
    probs = model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
    return [{"fraud_prob": round(float(p), 4),
             "decision": "review" if p > 0.5 else "approve"}
            for p in probs]
```

Run it and send a payment:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
pip install fastapi uvicorn
uvicorn app:app --port 8000

curl -X POST localhost:8000/score -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '[{"amount": 950, "hour": 3, "km_from_home": 400,
        "tx_last_hour": 5, "new_merchant": 1}]'
```

This is what happens inside, one request at a time:

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant F as FastAPI
  participant V as Pydantic
  participant M as Model
  C->>F: POST /score (JSON)
  F->>V: Validate fields
  alt invalid
    V-->>C: 422 error with field names
  else valid
    V->>M: DataFrame of payments
    M-->>F: Fraud probabilities
    F-->>C: 200 OK, decisions
  end
```

## Step 3: why batching matters

Every call to the model has a fixed overhead: Python function calls, input checks, memory setup. Scoring 1 row or 100 rows costs almost the same overhead. Here we time it live on the model we just trained.

```{python}
#| label: fig-batch
#| fig-cap: "Measured time per payment for different batch sizes on this machine. Larger batches spread the fixed overhead across many rows."
#| code-fold: true
import time, plotly.graph_objects as go
from ms_charts import COLORS, PLOTLY_CONFIG

sizes = [1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000]
per_row = []
for b in sizes:
    batch = Xte.iloc[:b]
    reps = max(3, 300 // b)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(reps):
        model.predict_proba(batch)
    per_row.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) / reps / b * 1000)   # ms per row

speedup = per_row[0] / per_row[-1]
fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=sizes, y=per_row, mode="lines+markers",
                           line=dict(color=COLORS["indigo"], width=3), marker=dict(size=9)))
fig.update_layout(height=360, xaxis=dict(type="log", title="Batch size (rows per call)"),
                  yaxis=dict(type="log", title="Milliseconds per payment"), showlegend=False)
fig.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG)
```

On this machine, scoring 1,000 payments in one call was about **`{python} f"{speedup:.0f}"`× cheaper per payment** than scoring them one at a time. Tools such as BentoML and Triton use **adaptive batching**: they wait a few milliseconds, collect requests that arrive together and score them as one batch. You trade a little latency for a lot of throughput. The [Scale](/deployment/scale/scaling-ml-inference.qmd) article explores this trade-off.

## Step 4: track and register with MLflow

When you train ten versions, you need to know which one is live and how it was made. MLflow records parameters, metrics and the model file, and keeps a **registry** of named versions ([MLflow docs](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/ml/model-registry/)).

::: {.panel-tabset}
## MLflow

```{.python filename="train_and_log.py"}
import mlflow, mlflow.sklearn

mlflow.set_experiment("payguard")
with mlflow.start_run():
    model = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=200).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    auc = roc_auc_score(yte, model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1])
    mlflow.log_param("max_iter", 200)
    mlflow.log_metric("auc", auc)
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, "model",
                             registered_model_name="payguard")
# browse runs: mlflow ui --port 5000
```

## BentoML

```{.python filename="service.py"}
import bentoml, joblib, pandas as pd

@bentoml.service(resources={"cpu": "2"})
class PayGuard:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model = joblib.load("models/payguard.joblib")

    @bentoml.api(batchable=True, max_batch_size=256)
    def score(self, rows: list[dict]) -> list[float]:
        X = pd.DataFrame(rows)
        return self.model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1].tolist()
# run: bentoml serve service:PayGuard
```

## Gradio demo

```{.python filename="demo.py"}
import gradio as gr, joblib, pandas as pd

model = joblib.load("models/payguard.joblib")

def check(amount, hour, km, tx, new):
    row = pd.DataFrame([[amount, hour, km, tx, int(new)]],
                       columns=model.feature_names_in_)
    return float(model.predict_proba(row)[0, 1])

gr.Interface(check,
             ["number", gr.Slider(0, 23, step=1), "number",
              "number", "checkbox"],
             "number", title="PayGuard demo").launch()
```
:::

```{ojs}
viewof needs = Inputs.checkbox(["Many model versions", "GPU deep learning", "Batching built in", "Quick demo for my team", "Already on Kubernetes", "Run on phones or edge"], {label: "I need", value: ["Many model versions"]})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const rec = new Set(["FastAPI"]);
  if (needs.includes("Many model versions")) rec.add("MLflow");
  if (needs.includes("GPU deep learning")) rec.add("NVIDIA Triton");
  if (needs.includes("Batching built in")) { rec.delete("FastAPI"); rec.add("BentoML"); }
  if (needs.includes("Quick demo for my team")) rec.add("Gradio");
  if (needs.includes("Already on Kubernetes")) rec.add("KServe");
  if (needs.includes("Run on phones or edge")) rec.add("ONNX Runtime");
  return html`<div class="ms-readout"><span>Start with</span><b>${[...rec].join(" + ")}</b><span>Add more only when a real need appears.</span></div>`;
}
```

## Common pitfalls

| Pitfall | What goes wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Loading the model inside the request | Every call reads the file from disk | Load once at start-up |
| No input validation | A missing field crashes the service | Use a Pydantic schema |
| Training and serving code differ | Features are computed differently, predictions drift | Share one feature function, or save a full `Pipeline` |
| Unpinned library versions | A model saved with one scikit-learn version fails to load in another | Pin versions in `requirements.txt` |
| No health endpoint | The platform cannot tell if the service is alive | Add `/health` |

## Summary

- Serving has four layers: **track, package, serve, demo**.
- **FastAPI** is the simplest door for a model; **BentoML** adds batching and packaging; **MLflow** tracks which version is which.
- Batching spreads fixed overhead across many rows, which made each payment about `{python} f"{speedup:.0f}"`× cheaper here.
- Next: automate training and testing with [MLOps pipelines](/deployment/mlops/mlops-pipelines.qmd).
